Oct. 13th: The Florida Panthers have recalled some goaltending depth ahead of tonight’s contest against the Columbus Blue Jackets. According to the AHL transactions log , the Panthers recalled netminder Cooper Black from the AHL’s Charlotte Checkers. It’s already clear why Florida recalled Black. In last night’s game against the Buffalo Sabres, the Panthers pulled Jacob Markström after the first period. Following the loss, rinkside reporter Katie Engleson quoted head coach Paul Maurice , saying, “ [H]e just tightened up, so we pulled him. We don’t think….there’s no injury there…just standard stuff. ” Because they will play in the second half of a back-to-back tonight, Florida appears to be playing it safe with Markström. Black, 25, has been in the Panthers organization for the past four years. He signed as a collegiate free agent from Dartmouth College toward the end of the 2023-24 campaign. If he sees any action against the Columbus Blue Jackets this evening, it will be Black’s NHL debut. During his rookie season, Black split his time between the AHL and ECHL, but last year he played exclusively in the AHL. It was a relatively successful season, as the Alpena, MI native finished 25-13-4 in 42 games with a .903 SV% and 2.47 GAA. He’s had similar production to start the 2026-27 season, managing a 1-1-0 record through his first two games with a .906 SV% and 3.01 GAA.

items.body: Allowing third-most goals-against in NHL entering game against Rangers Saturday Rick Bowness said everyone associated with the Columbus Blue Jackets "should be very angry with where we are." The coach, speaking on Friday, said he especially was bothered by the fact that the Blue Jackets have allowed an average of 4.20 goals per game, tied for the third most in the NHL. "We're 30th in the League in goals-against -- 30th," Bowness said. "I've never coached a team that was 30th in the League in goals-against." The Blue Jackets (2-3-0), who host the New York Rangers at Nationwide Arena on Saturday (7 p.m. ET; CBJHN, CBJNHL, MSG), haven't played since Tuesday, a 7-3 home loss to the Florida Panthers. That followed a 5-3 loss at the St. Louis Blues on Saturday. They have allowed at least three goals in four of their five games and are 1-3-0 after a 6-3 win against the Buffalo Sabres in their season opener Oct. 1. After the loss to the Panthers, Bowness voiced his frustration with his team. "We beat ourselves in St. Louis. We beat ourselves tonight," Bowness said. "So you have to hope, you've got to believe, that that performance tonight will embarrass them enough to stop this, right? Because if they're not embarrassed by that, we don't want them on the team. It's as simple as that. "I'm not a babysitter. I'm too old to be a babysitter for these guys. You're a professional athlete, prepare yourself to play properly." This is not the first time that Bowness has called out his team. Last season, after the Blue Jackets had been eliminated from Stanley Cup Playoff contention, Bowness said if he returned to Columbus this season, he would be "changing the culture." items.title: Why are teams struggling to sell out games?
items.summary: The Vegas Golden Knights snapped a nine-year sellout streak this season.
items.body: Add to Preferred Sources Credit: Bob Frid-Imagn Images The NHL is a gate-driven league. You may have heard this said a time or two before. While leagues like the NFL and NBA generate a major portion of their revenue from broadcasting deals, the NHL still relies much more heavily on in-person attendance. It can’t be a great sign, then, that teams around the league have been failing to sell out early in the season. The Vegas Golden Knights snapped their nine-year sellout streak on October 8, when they hit just 92% attendance for a game against the Toronto Maple Leafs . On Thursday, the Edmonton Oilers had over 2,000 empty seats for their home game against the Utah Mammoth . Multiple other teams have seen their attendance fall short of expectations. On Friday’s episode of Daily Faceoff LIVE , hosts Tyler Yaremchuk and Carter Hutton discussed the possible reasons for the disappointing attendance figures across the NHL. Tyler Yaremchuk: If you go back to Tuesday, I saw this from Puck Report NHL, of the 16 home games, because remember on Tuesday every single team in the NHL played, there were just as many teams that were sub-90% attendance as there were at 100% and sold out, which I just think is crazy. The Blue Jackets were at 75%, the Islanders were at 79%, the Senators were at 82%, the Sharks were at 82%. Last night in Edmonton, they were at 82% capacity for a Thursday night game. items.title: Ducks’ rebuild provides blueprint for Flames to follow
items.summary: As the Flames embark on their own rebuild, the Ducks are beginning to look an awful lot like the blueprint GM Craig Conroy would love to follow, writes Eric Francis.
items.body: That was the timeline Pat Verbeek had in mind shortly after he took the wheel in Anaheim, a franchise that needed to tear things down before it could dream of building something special again. The goal wasn't to win a Stanley Cup in five years. It wasn't even to guarantee a playoff spot. It was to become a team that could start contending for a sprinkling of spring hockey. As the Calgary Flames embark on their own uncomfortable transition, Verbeek's Anaheim Ducks are beginning to look an awful lot like the blueprint Craig Conroy would love to follow. The similarities aren't lost on Verbeek, who has watched his young Ducks take a significant step forward after years of accumulating draft picks, developing talent and carefully adding veterans to help the kids grow. "When I talk to Connie, yeah," Verbeek said of the parallels between Anaheim's rebuild and Calgary's. "Transitioning is probably the hardest thing to do, not wanting to take a step back, but just kind of gaining a little ground every year.” In a one-on-one chat outside the Ducks dressing room, Verbeek said that when he arrived in Anaheim in Feb. 2022, his first instinct was to try to retain the veteran foundation on a team that missed the playoffs three years running. But Josh Manson, Hampus Lindholm and Rickard Rakell couldn't be signed to new deals, forcing the general manager to change course. That pivot, as he calls it, became the foundation of the rebuild. Rather than cling to a group that wasn't going to take the Ducks where they wanted to go, Verbeek traded those veterans and began stockpiling draft picks, putting an emphasis on identifying and developing young talent. items.body: Register Login Seattle Kraken Recall Ty Nelson By Brennan McClain | at October 16, 2026 1:00 pm The Seattle Kraken have recalled defensive reinforcements after Brandon Montour suffered a lower-body injury last night. According to a team announcement , the Kraken recalled defenseman Ty Nelson from the AHL’s Coachella Valley Firebirds. Seattle had an open roster spot before the transaction, so no corresponding roster move was necessary. Seattle selected Nelson, 22, with the 68th overall pick (third-round) in the 2022 NHL Draft. The Toronto, ON, native played for the OHL’s North Bay Battalion at the time, scoring 40 goals and 128 points in 121 games in his two post-draft campaigns. Nelson has continued his strong two-way play in the AHL. Since debuting with AHL Coachella Valley in 2024-25, he has registered 17 goals and 71 points in 140 games with a +34 rating. He has puck-moving skills similar to those of other smaller defensemen. Still, despite standing at 5’10″and weighing 198 lbs, Nelson plays extremely large. They aren’t all bone-crushing hits, but he plays with an extremely high motor and sacrifices his body almost every shift. Unfortunately, despite his strong play with the Firebirds, Nelson hasn’t made his NHL debut. Depending on the severity of Montour’s injury, that could change during his current recall. Even without Montour, Seattle maintains a solid mix of handedness in their defensive corps. They could consider removing Cale Fleury for a game or two to provide Nelson with an opportunity.

items.title: ‘Should all be very angry’: Cooler heads not prevailing for Blue Jackets’ Bowness
items.body: The Columbus Blue Jackets coach continued his public tirade over his team's defence on Friday three days after it suffered a 7-3 loss to the Floridaa Panthers. "Right now, we should all be very angry at where we are," Bowness told reporters . "You look at our team. We’re 30th in the league in goals against. I’ve never coached a team that was 30th in the league in goals against … I’m mad. I keep seeing 30th goals against. That bothers me." Columbus, which sits 3-2 on the season, is tied with the Los Angeles Kings for third-last in the NHL at 4.20 goals against per game. The Blue Jackets fell apart in the second period of the Panthers loss, allowing four goals including a natural hat trick from Brady Tkachuk. Forward Mathieu Olivier did his team no favours either, taking an ill-advised five-minute major penalty for slashing, which led to his subsequent ejection and another goal against. "Yeah. They’re like I am. They’re not happy where they are," he said. The 71-year-old coach ripped into his players in the immediate aftermath of the game on Tuesday, calling the performance "embarrassing." "You gotta believe that performance will embarrass them enough to stop this, right?" Bowness told reporters . "Because if they're not embarrassed by that, we don't want them on the team. Simple as that." "I know it looks bad, but I believe in what we're doing. I believe in them. I believe we can fix the problems," the bench boss added. "That all being said, if (the game) doesn't get their attention, then they're on the wrong team." Blue Jackets players will have their first chance to do just that when they return to the ice Saturday for a home date against the New York Rangers.

items.body: Add to Preferred Sources Credit: Isaiah J. Downing-Imagn Images The Central Division is widely regarded as the toughest division in the NHL, and the early going shows that a few teams can be Stanley Cup Playoff contenders. The Colorado Avalanche certainly set the pace last year, getting off to an incredible start before running away with the Presidents’ Trophy. The Dallas Stars and Minnesota Wild weren’t all that far behind them, with the Wild showing they can be one of the top teams in the division if they get hot at the right time. In the early stages of the 2026-27 season, there’s certainly been a surprise in how the teams in the division have played. The Stars have struggled, and the Avs don’t look nearly as strong. items.summary: So Gavin McKenna was benched on Thursday and played less than seven minutes against the Sabres. Justin Bourne takes a detailed look at what the 18-year-old did with his ice time to try and make sense of the benching.
items.body: In the midst of a close divisional game against the Buffalo Sabres, Gavin McKenna found himself stapled to the bench from halfway through the second period through to the final buzzer. He played just 6:36 in total. To my memory, it was one of the longest benchings of a non-fourth line player in years in Toronto, and given it happened to their recent number one overall draft pick, we’re going to talk about it. We’re going to talk about it partially because it’s McKenna, who at times has been electric in his first eight NHL games. But we're also going to talk about it because it felt like a microcosm of a strategic coaching problem in the loss. They stapled talent to the bench while increasing the minutes for their defensive veterans, trying to hold on to a two-goal lead rather than continuing to take it to a Sabres team whose blue line – without Rasmus Dahlin – was badly struggling to manage the Leafs' talent up-front. So, the kid played under seven minutes, and didn't see the ice at all in the game’s second half. Why? There are four possible reasons, one of which is the explanation Jim Hiller gave, which would be the most damning of all for the staff. items.summary: Does GM Danny Briere stay the course or try to shake up his team?
items.body: Add to Preferred Sources Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The horrific start to the season for the Philadelphia Flyers has definitely got the hockey world talking. Head coach Rick Tocchet’s job is being questioned; rumors are swirling about winger Travis Konecny; management’s vision is being scrutinized. All this to say, the times are turbulent for the Orange and Black. Following their loss Thursday night, the team is now 0-6-3 to start the season. So no better time to turn it over to the fans, right? Let’s jump into the latest NHL mailbag, with the Flyers taking center stage. Further to what I wrote on Tuesday , it wasn’t connecting dots, but rather two things that were said by a team source. It was directly pointed out that Travis Konecny has been a constant on the Flyers’ dismal power play over the last number of seasons, but that alone is not the reason as to why he would be approached about waiving his no-movement clause. Yes, the Flyers have internal frustrations with his play going back to last season’s playoffs, but approaching him about waiving his NMC would be a result of this season continuing to spiral and the team looking to make a major change to the roster. Konecny has led the team in scoring the last number of seasons and is still an effective player; moving him would be more about a team-identity shift and parlaying a (presumably) coveted asset on the trade market into something that could help the team (like a young center). items.body: Register Login Midday Notes: Raddysh, Back, Xhekaj By Marcus Antonelli | at October 16, 2026 11:26 am The New York Rangers have recalled Taylor Raddysh from Hartford, their AHL affiliate, and have sent down Jaroslav Chmelar . Raddysh joins the team having played the start of his 2026-27 campaign with three goals for five points in five AHL contests. The former second-round pick is in the second year of a two-year, $1.5MM AAV contract. At age 28, Raddysh has solidified his professional profile as a depth piece for an organization that can provide some worthy second-hand offense. In his first year with New York, he scored 19 points in 68 games. Historically, Raddysh has seen a near 40-point campaign with the Blackhawks back in 2022-23. Even then, penalty killing and defensive prowess are valuable things the Rangers will need out of him, which he has been prominent in. Chmelar, in comparison, has been averaging less NHL time than what Raddysh usually provides in a similar role. The former fifth-round pick out of Czechia has started his first seven NHL games in 2026-27 with around eight minutes of ice time at 5-on-5 and has yet to produce a point. The 23-year-old has fared better in the AHL, having scored 56 points across three seasons, totaling 124 games. He could benefit from more minutes, similar to how Cole Beaudoin wouldn’t receive quality NHL ice time yet. He’s known as a forward who attacks straight with his speed, but has areas to improve in his handling, which, if mastered, could help with more offensive opportunities.

items.body: Forward to play 20th NHL season, spent 2025-26 with Senators, Red Wings David Perron signed a one-year, $850,000 contract with the Dallas Stars on Friday. The 38-year-old forward had 28 points (13 goals, 15 assists) in 65 regular-season games for the Ottawa Senators and Detroit Red Wings last season, including three goals in 16 games with Detroit after he was acquired in a trade March 5. "We watched him (Thursday)," Stars coach Glen Gulutzan said. "Obviously the veteran presence is there and his actual paly, just how good he is along the walls.
